claims.text: High-cooling-rate processing can preserve a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution in Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy has Mg uniformly distributed throughout the matrix.
The rapidly cooled metastable state has elevated free energy.
Thermal aging destabilizes the metastable solid solution.
During thermal exposure, Mg diffuses out of the matrix and segregates.
Mg segregation drives nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially form at grain boundaries and dislocation accumulations.
Intermetallic precipitation modifies the local chemistry at grain boundaries and other critical microstructural locations.
The resulting local chemical changes interfere with formation or stability of a consistent protective oxide or passive film.
Changes in protective-film formation or stability alter corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
After identical aging, high-cooling-rate samples will contain a higher density and more continuous distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases than slower-cooled samples.
Aging-induced intermetallic formation will correlate with altered, most likely reduced, corrosion performance relative to the initial metastable state.
Aging-induced intermetallic formation will correlate with altered, most likely reduced, oxidation performance relative to the initial metastable state.
The two processing routes will exhibit measurably different onset kinetics for intermetallic formation.
Below a temperature-time threshold for pronounced Mg segregation, the metastable state will be retained.
Above that temperature-time threshold, significant intermetallic formation will occur.
